officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings and their numbering (1 to 10, 1.1 to 8.3) are transcribed from the subject content of the official syllabus. Objective codes are the board's statement numbers (subtopic or topic code plus the statement number and letter, e.g. 1.1.4b, 7.5a). Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; no syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Read on 2026-10-08: the syllabus for examination in 2026, 2027 and 2028 (the cover says version 6; the back-page copyright line still reads September 2023) and the separate syllabus update notice for version 6 (September 2026). The update lists the changes since version 1: v6 (September 2026) updated the description of the ROUND library routine (it rounds a real value or expression to a given number of decimal places; ROUND(RANDOM() * 6, 0) gives a whole number from 0 to 6, and RANDOM() returns a number between 0 and 1 inclusive); v5 changed a web link only; v4 updated operator names and allowed procedures and functions up to three parameters; v3 updated operator names; v2 clarified that Paper 2 solutions involving code must be in pseudocode, except the 15-mark scenario question, which may be answered in pseudocode, Python, Visual Basic or Java. The text read already contains these changes; objectives 8.1.6b and 8.1.7 and the components below reflect them.

Assessment as read: all candidates take Paper 1 Computer Systems (1 hour 45 minutes, 75 marks, 50%: short-answer and structured questions on topics 1-6) and Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic (1 hour 45 minutes, 75 marks, 50%: short-answer and structured questions on topics 7-10, ending with a 15-mark unseen scenario question of about 30 minutes in which candidates write an algorithm in pseudocode or program code). All questions are compulsory; calculators are not allowed in either paper; grades A* to G. Assessment objectives: AO1 40%, AO2 40%, AO3 20% overall (Paper 1 60/20/20, Paper 2 20/60/20).

Section 4 of the syllabus sets the flowchart symbols, logic gate symbols and pseudocode conventions used in the examination (assignment with a left arrow, upper-case keywords, Pascal-case identifiers, DECLARE, CONSTANT, IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF, CASE OF ... OTHERWISE ... ENDCASE, FOR ... NEXT, WHILE ... ENDWHILE, REPEAT ... UNTIL, PROCEDURE/FUNCTION with RETURNS, OPENFILE/READFILE/WRITEFILE/CLOSEFILE). The platform shows no symbol images: content describes gates and flowcharts in words or tables and writes pseudocode in those conventions.

Mathematical requirements as read: arithmetic, averages, random numbers, decimals, fractions, percentages and ratios, positive and negative integers and real numbers, number systems, counting, totalling and rounding, all without a calculator.

Sharing with ZIMSEC: concepts shared with the ZIMSEC syllabus are taught at Cambridge depth; ZIMSEC-only concepts (octal, binary subtraction, networks and topologies, applications, systems analysis, web design, technopreneurship and others) are not covered by this file.
overview: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science has two halves. Computer systems (topics 1-6): data representation, data transmission, hardware, software, the internet and its uses, and automated and emerging technologies. Algorithms, programming and logic (topics 7-10): algorithm design and problem-solving, programming in pseudocode, databases and SQL, and Boolean logic. Learners are expected to write, run, test and debug their own programs.
assessmentOverview: Two compulsory written papers, each 1 hour 45 minutes, 75 marks and 50%, no calculators: Paper 1 Computer Systems (topics 1-6) and Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic (topics 7-10), which ends with a 15-mark scenario question answered in pseudocode, Python, Visual Basic or Java.

components.name: Paper 1: Computer Systems
components.description: Compulsory short-answer and structured questions on topics 1-6.

components.name: Paper 2: Algorithms, Programming and Logic
components.description: Compulsory short-answer and structured questions on topics 7-10, ending with a 15-mark unseen scenario question (pseudocode or Python, Visual Basic or Java).

objectives.text: Understand how and why computers use binary to represent all forms of data.
Understand the denary, binary and hexadecimal number systems.
Convert positive integers (up to 16 bits) between denary and binary, denary and hexadecimal, and hexadecimal and binary.
Explain why hexadecimal is a useful representation and identify where it is used.
Add two positive 8-bit binary integers.
Explain overflow and why it happens in binary addition.
Carry out single and multiple logical shifts on a positive 8-bit integer and describe their effect.
Represent positive and negative 8-bit integers in two's complement and convert to and from it.
Explain how text is represented using character sets, including ASCII and Unicode.
Explain how sound is represented and the effect of sample rate and sample resolution.
Explain how images are represented and the effect of resolution and colour depth.
Use the units of data storage from the bit to the exbibyte, with 1024 between units.
Calculate the file size of an image file and a sound file from given information.
Explain the purpose of and need for data compression.
Explain how lossy and lossless compression (including run-length encoding) reduce file size.

children.name: Types and methods of data transmission

objectives.text: Understand that data is split into packets for transmission.
Describe the structure of a packet: header, payload and trailer.
Describe packet switching.
Describe serial, parallel, simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex transmission.
Explain which transmission method suits a given scenario.
Explain how the USB interface transmits data, with its benefits and drawbacks.
Explain why data is checked for errors after transmission and how errors occur.
Describe parity checks (odd and even, parity byte and parity block), checksums and echo checks.
Describe how a check digit detects data-entry errors, with examples such as ISBNs and bar codes.
Describe how an automatic repeat query uses acknowledgements and timeouts.
Explain why data is encrypted when it is transmitted.
Explain symmetric and asymmetric encryption, including public and private keys.
Explain the role of the CPU.
Explain what a microprocessor is.
Explain the purpose of the units, registers and buses of a Von Neumann CPU.
Describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle and the part each component plays.
Explain how cores, cache and the clock affect CPU performance.
Explain the purpose of an instruction set.
Describe embedded systems and identify devices that use them.
Explain what an input device is and why it is needed.
Explain what an output device is and why it is needed.
Explain what a sensor is and what sensors are used for.
Identify the data each sensor captures and choose the most suitable sensor for a context.
Explain primary storage, including the roles of RAM and ROM.
Explain secondary storage.
Describe how magnetic, optical and solid-state storage work, with examples.
Describe virtual memory: how it is created and used and why it is needed.
Explain cloud storage.
Compare storing data in the cloud with storing it locally.
Explain why a computer needs a network interface card to access a network.
Explain the purpose and structure of a MAC address.
Explain the purpose of an IP address.
Compare static and dynamic addresses and IPv4 and IPv6.
Describe the role of a router in a network.
Distinguish system software from application software, with examples.
Describe the role and basic functions of an operating system.
Explain how hardware, firmware and an operating system are needed to run applications.
Describe how interrupts are generated and handled, and their effect.

children.name: Types of programming language, translators and integrated development environments (IDEs)

objectives.text: Explain high-level and low-level languages and the advantages and disadvantages of each.
Explain that assembly language uses mnemonics and needs an assembler.
Describe how a compiler and an interpreter translate code and report errors.
Explain the advantages and disadvantages of compilers and interpreters.
Explain the role and common functions of an IDE.

children.name: The internet and the world wide web

objectives.text: Distinguish the internet from the world wide web.
Explain what a URL is and its parts.
Describe the purpose and operation of HTTP and HTTPS.
Explain the purpose and functions of a web browser.
Describe how a web page is located, retrieved and displayed when a URL is entered.
Explain session and persistent cookies and how cookies are used.
Explain what a digital currency is and how it is used.
Explain how blockchain tracks digital currency transactions.
Describe how a range of cyber security threats are carried out and what they aim to do.
Explain how a range of solutions help keep data safe from these threats.
Describe how sensors, microprocessors and actuators work together in automated systems.
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of an automated system in a given scenario.
Explain what robotics is.
Describe the characteristics of a robot.
Describe the roles of robots and the advantages and disadvantages of their use.
Explain what artificial intelligence is.
Describe the main characteristics of AI: data and rules, reasoning, and learning and adapting.
Explain the basic operation and components of expert systems and machine learning.
Identify the stages of the program development life cycle (analysis, design, coding, testing) and the tasks in each.
Understand that a computer system is made of sub-systems.
Decompose a problem into its component parts (inputs, processes, outputs, storage).
Design solutions with structure diagrams, flowcharts and pseudocode.
State the purpose of a given algorithm and describe its processes.
Use the standard methods: linear search, bubble sort, totalling, counting, and maximum, minimum and average.
Explain the need for validation and use range, length, type, presence, format and check-digit checks.
Explain the need for verification and use visual and double-entry checks.
Suggest and apply normal, abnormal, extreme and boundary test data.
Complete a trace table for a dry run of an algorithm.
Identify errors in an algorithm and suggest corrections.
Write and amend algorithms in pseudocode, program code and flowcharts for given problems.
Declare and use variables and constants.
Use the integer, real, char, string and Boolean data types.
Use input and output.
Use sequence.
Use selection with IF and CASE statements.
Use count-controlled, pre-condition and post-condition loops.
Use totalling and counting.
Use string handling: length, substring, upper and lower case.
Use arithmetic, relational and logical operators.
Use nested selection and iteration (up to three levels).
Explain procedures, functions and parameters.
Define and use procedures and functions with or without parameters (up to three).
Use local and global variables.
Use the library routines MOD, DIV, ROUND and RANDOM.
Create maintainable programs with meaningful identifiers, comments, procedures and functions.
Declare and use one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays.
Explain the use of arrays.
Write values into and read values from an array using iteration, including nested iteration.
Explain why programs store data in files.
Open, close, read from and write to a file (single items and lines of text).
Define a single-table database (fields, records, validation) from given requirements.
Suggest suitable basic data types for fields.
Explain the purpose of a primary key and choose a suitable one.
Read, complete and write SQL scripts that query a single table (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, SUM, COUNT, AND, OR) and state their output.
Identify and use the standard symbols for the NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR and XOR gates.
Define the function of each logic gate and its output for every input combination.
Create a logic circuit from a problem statement, a logic expression or a truth table.
Complete a truth table from a problem statement, a logic expression or a logic circuit.
Write a logic expression from a problem statement, a logic circuit or a truth table.
